explanation: Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent because R2.A is the primary key, so Y.A=Z.A implies Y and Z are the same row, making Y.B=Z.B always true and X.A=Z.A redundant in both queries.

q1: SELECT * FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.ITEMN IN (SELECT ITL.ITEMN FROM ITL ITL WHERE ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.* FROM ITP ITP, ITL ITL WHERE ITP.ITEMN = ITL.ITEMN AND ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0

Since ITP has a primary key on ITEMN, ensuring no duplicates, and both approaches effectively perform a semi-join, they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X WHERE (X.PNUM, X.QOH) IN (SELECT Y.PNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CNT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10)
q2: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X, (SELECT Y.PNUM AS SUPPNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10 GROUP BY Y.PNUM) TEMP WHERE X.QOH = TEMP.CT AND X.PNUM = TEMP.SUPPNUM
schema:
CREATE TABLE PARTS (PNUM INT, QOH INT);
CREATE TABLE SUPPLY (PNUM INT, SHIPDATE INT);
explanation: Q1 is invalid in standard SQL due to the missing GROUP BY clause in the subquery, which prevents proper aggregation by PNUM. Even if executed, Q1's subquery returns a single row with an arbitrary PNUM and the total count of SUPPLY records with SHIPDATE < 10, while Q2 correctly groups by PNUM and returns the count per PNUM. This leads to different results when multiple PNUMs exist in SUPPLY with SHIPDATE < 10.
counterexample: INSERT INTO PARTS (PNUM, QOH) VALUES (1, 2); INSERT INTO PARTS (PNUM, QOH) VALUES (2, 1); INSERT INTO SUPPLY (PNUM, SHIPDATE) VALUES (1, 5); INSERT INTO SUPPLY (PNUM, SHIPDATE) VALUES (2, 5);
counterexample_dsp: With PARTS containing (1,2) and (2,1), and SUPPLY containing (1,5) and (2,5) (both SHIPDATE < 10), Q1 may return XP=1 (if the subquery arbitrarily returns (1,2)) while Q2 returns XP=2.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 aim to find departments with an average instructor salary greater than 50000, but they differ in the HAVING clause: Q1 requires exactly 4 distinct salaries in the department, while Q2 requires more than 4 distinct salaries. This significant difference in logic means the queries are not semantically equivalent, as they can select different sets of departments based on the count of distinct salaries.
counterexample_dsp: A department with exactly 4 distinct instructor salaries and an average salary greater than 50000. Q1 includes this department due to COUNT(DISTINCT SALARY)=4, but Q2 excludes it because COUNT(DISTINCT SALARY) is not greater than 4.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY STUDENT.ID,STUDENT.DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY STUDENT.ID HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent because grouping by STUDENT.ID alone or with STUDENT.DEPT_NAME does not change the groups, as DEPT_NAME is functionally dependent on ID in the joined result. The HAVING clause COUNT(DEPT_NAME) counts the number of rows per group, which is identical in both cases.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT COURSE_ID)>4)
q2: SELECT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT COURSE_ID)>4)
explanation: Q1 uses SELECT DISTINCT to remove duplicate department names, while Q2 does not. This means that if multiple courses in the same department have credits equal to the maximum credits from the subquery, Q2 will output duplicate department names, whereas Q1 will output each department name only once.
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES (1, 1, 1000); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 1, 1, 5); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (2, 1, 1, 5); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (3, 1, 1, 5); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (4, 1, 1, 5); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (5, 1, 1, 5);
counterexample_dsp: A database with one department (DEPT_NAME=1) that has exactly five distinct courses with TITLE=1 (representing 'CS'), all with CREDITS=5. The subquery returns MAX(CREDITS)=5 for this department. Q2 outputs five rows of DEPT_NAME=1, while Q1 outputs one row.

explanation: Both queries have an outer HAVING clause with COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2, which is always false when grouping by STUDENT.ID (as ID is constant per group), so both always return empty results regardless of the subquery differences.

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1's subquery groups by both year and course_id, filtering on per-course count of instructor entries, while Q2 groups only by year, filtering on overall year count. q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A ON COURSE.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(C.CID) > 1000
explanation: Q1 groups by carrier name and full date (year, month, day), requiring flight count >1000 per specific date, while Q2 groups by carrier name and day of month only, requiring total flights per day number >1000. Thus, Q2 can output carriers that have no single date with over 1000 flights but have a day number with total over 1000, making Q2 a superset of Q1.
counterexample_dsp: A carrier with CID=1 and NAME=1 has 1000 flights on 2020-01-01 (YEAR=2020, MONTH_ID=1, DAY_OF_MONTH=1) and 1 flight on 2020-02-01 (YEAR=2020, MONTH_ID=2, DAY_OF_MONTH=1). Q1 outputs nothing as no group has count>1000, but Q2 outputs the carrier name since the group for day 1 has count=1001>1000.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.CID, C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 groups by carrier ID, name, and specific date (year, month, day), counting flights per carrier per specific day, while Q2 groups only by carrier name and day of month, counting flights per carrier name per day of month across all years and months. q2: SELECT S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY) AS S JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON S.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY AND F2.ACTUAL_TIME = S.MAX_TIME GROUP BY S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY
explanation: Both queries find for each origin city the destinations with flights having the maximum actual time for that origin, and output the origin, destination, and that time. The distinct in Q1 and group by in Q2 handle duplicates similarly, resulting in equivalent outputs.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT P.ORIGIN_CITY, P.DEST_CITY, P.ACTUAL_TIME FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON F1.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS P WHERE P.ACTUAL_TIME = P.MAX_ACTUAL_TIME

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 groups by YEAR and COURSE_ID in the inner query, summing YEAR multiplied by the number of courses per year with over 4 instructors, while Q2 groups only by YEAR, summing YEAR for each year with total over 4 instructors, leading to different sums when multiple courses per year meet the condition.
counterexample_dsp: For year 2020, with two courses (101 and 102) each taught by 5 instructors, Q1 sums 2020 twice (4040) while Q2 sums it once (2020).

q1: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE
q2: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS > 3
explanation: Q1 selects all courses, while Q2 only selects courses with credits greater than 3. They are not equivalent because Q2 excludes courses with credits <= 3 or NULL.
counterexample: INSERT INTO COURSE VALUES (1, 101, 1, 4); INSERT INTO COURSE VALUES (2, 102, 1, 3);
counterexample_dsp: A test database with two courses: one with credits 4 (included in both Q1 and Q2) and one with credits 3 (included only in Q1).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
q2: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
explanation: Q1 uses an equality join on COURSE_ID, returning only courses directly taught in 2010. Q2 uses a range join (>=) which can include courses not taught in 2010 if their ID is higher, leading to incorrect pairings and extra rows.
counterexample: INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (101, 1, 1, 3); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (102, 2, 1, 3); INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES (1, 101, 1, 2010, 1, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Test data with two courses (IDs 101 and 102) and one teaches record (course ID 101, year 2010). Q1 returns only course 101 with its instructor, while Q2 incorrectly includes course 102 paired with the same instructor.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR LEFT OUTER JOIN TEACHES ON INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR, TEACHES WHERE INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN with an inequality condition (INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID), which can include instructors even if no matching TEACHES record exists or if TEACHES records have smaller IDs, while Q2 uses an inner join on equality (INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID), which only includes instructors with exact ID matches in TEACHES.
counterexample: INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES (2, 1, 0, 0); INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES (1, 101, 0, 0, 0, 0);
counterexample_dsp: When an instructor has an ID greater than a TEACHES ID but not equal to any TEACHES ID, Q1 returns a row with the instructor's details and the COURSE_ID from a TEACHES record with a smaller ID, while Q2 returns no rows for that instructor.

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: Both queries group by ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR, making COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) always 1 per group. Thus, HAVING conditions >4 and >5 are both false, resulting in empty outputs for both queries.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS=(SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE AS C JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A WHERE C.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 selects departments that have at least one course with the global maximum credits across all courses, while Q2 selects departments that have at least one course with the maximum credits within that department. Since the global maximum may differ from department-wise maximums, the queries are not equivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO COURSE VALUES (1, 1, 1, 4); INSERT INTO COURSE VALUES (2, 2, 1, 3); INSERT INTO COURSE VALUES (3, 3, 2, 5); INSERT INTO COURSE VALUES (4, 4, 2, 2);
counterexample_dsp: In a test database with two departments: DeptA has courses with credits 3 and 4 (department max is 4), and DeptB has courses with credits 2 and 5 (department max is 5, and global max is 5). Q1 returns only DeptB, while Q2 returns both DeptA and DeptB.
